# Problem 1: NY NOAA

## 1.0. Load `ny_noaa` Dataset

```{r load-ny-noaa}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

## 1.1. Data Description

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains daily weather data from `r min(pull(ny_noaa, date))` to `r max(pull(ny_noaa, date))` in `r n_distinct(pull(ny_noaa, id))` different weather stations across New York State, resulting in `r nrow(ny_noaa)` total observations (one row per weather station per day). There are `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables in the dataset: the weather station ID (`id`), the date of observation (`date`), daily precipitation (`prcp`, in tenths of mm), daily snowfall (`snow`, in mm), daily snow depth (`snwd`, in mm), and maximum and minimum daily temperature (`tmax` and `tmin`, in tenths of a degreee Celcuius). Weather station ID and date are never missing, but missing data is a substantial issue for the weather measurements: `r round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp))) * 100, 2)`% of precipitation values, `r round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow))) * 100, 2)`% of snowfall values, `r round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snwd))) * 100, 2)`% of snow depth values, and `r round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax))) * 100, 2)`% and `r round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmin))) * 100, 2)`% of respective maximum and minimum temperature values are missing.

## 1.2. Data Cleaning

```{r clean-noaa}
noaa = ny_noaa |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), "-") |>
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp/10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10,
    year = as.numeric(year),
    month = as.numeric(month),
    day = as.numeric(day)
    )
```

After cleaning the `ny_noaa` dataset, `year`, `month`, and `day` are separate numeric variables. Precipitation was converted from tenths of mm to mm, and maximum and minimum temperature were converted from tenths of a degree to degrees Celsius.

## 1.3. Frequency of `snowfall` Values

```{r snow-freq-rank}
snow_freq_df = noaa |>
  group_by(snow) |>
  summarise(n_obs = n()) |>
  mutate(snow_freq_rank = min_rank(desc(n_obs)))
```

For snowfall, the most common value of ``r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 1), snow)`` mm occurred across `r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 1), n_obs)` observations. This is due to the fact that it does not snow on most days of the year and usually only during certain months of the year. The second most common value of ``r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 2), snow)`` occurred across `r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 2), n_obs)` observations. This is due to the fact that some weather stations only recorded precipitation data. The next most common values are `r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 3), snow)`, `r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 4), snow)`, `r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 4), snow)`, and `r pull(filter(snow_freq_df, snow_freq_rank == 5), snow)` mm. These correspond to 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches, which suggests that many weather stations measure snowfall in inches and the values were converted to mm afterward.

## 1.4. Average `tmax` in January and July

```{r avg-tmax-plot}
noaa |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>
  group_by(id, month, year) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm=TRUE)) |>
  mutate(
    month = case_match(month, 
                      1 ~ "January", 
                      7 ~ "July")
    ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = .8) +
  geom_line(alpha = .1) +
  facet_grid(month ~ .) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July, by Station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum daily temperature (°C)",
    caption = "Data from the ny_noaa dataset")
```

Visually inspecting the *Average Maximum Temperature in January and July, by Station** indicates that `January` is consistently much colder than July. Most weather station's `tmax` averages fall between about -10°C and 10°C in January and between about 20°C and 33°C in July. There is clear year-to-year structure, since average maximum temperatures of stations tend to rise and fall together. For example, January was unusually cold across most stations in 1994 and 2004 and unusually warm in 1990 and 2006. January averages also vary more between years than July averages.  There are a few noticeable outliers, including one weather station with an average July maximum of only about 14°C in 1988, and two with average January maximums of about -13°C (1982) and -12°C (2005).

## 1.5. `tmax` vs. `tmin`; Snowfall Distribution

```{r temp-snow-facets}
ggp_tmax_tmin = noaa |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum daily temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum daily temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Number of days",) +  
    theme(legend.text = element_text(angle = 90))

ggp_snow_ridge = noaa |> 
  filter(snow > 0 & snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = factor(year))) + 
  geom_density_ridges(scale = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Snowfall (0-100 mm) by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year",
    caption = "Data from the ny_noaa dataset")

ggp_tmax_tmin + ggp_snow_ridge
```

Maximum and minimum daily temperature are strongly and positively related. The most frequent `tmax` and `tmin` combinations are in the range of about (-10°C, 0°C) to (20°C, 30°C), with `tmax` usually about 5-15°C warmer than `tmin`. There are a few outliers that seem implausible and might be a result of measurement errors. For example, there are days with `tmax` values of 60°C, and `r nrow(filter(noaa, tmin > tmax))` days have a `tmin` greater than `tmax`.

The distribution of daily snowfall (excluding days with no snow) looks consistent from year to year. In every year, most snowfall days have less than about 30 mm of `snow`, and the distributions have peaks at about 13, 25, 51, and 76 mm, which matches the measurements-by-inch and conversion to mm approach alluded to earlier. 

# Problem 2: MIMS

## 2.1. Load, tidy, merge into `mims`

```{r mims-load-tidy-merge}
mims_demos = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", 
           skip = 4,
           na = c("NA")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    seqn = as.character(seqn),
    sex = case_match(sex, 
                     1 ~ "male", 
                     2 ~ "female"),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    education = case_match(education, 
                           1 ~ "less than high school",
                           2 ~ "high school equivalent",
                           3 ~ "more than high school"),
    education = factor(education, 
                       levels = c("less than high school", 
                                  "high school equivalent", 
                                  "more than high school")
                       )
    )

mims_accel = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")|>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(seqn = as.character(seqn)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute", 
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
    ) |>
  mutate(minute = as.integer(minute))

mims = left_join(mims_demos, mims_accel, by = "seqn") |>
       select(seqn, minute, mims, everything())
```

## 2.2. `mims` Data Visualization 

### 2.2.1. Frequency by `sex` & `education`

```{r mims-freq-table}
mims |> 
  distinct(seqn, sex, education) |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Based on the frequency table, the largest `education` group is more than high school, with similar numbers of males and females. The less than high school `education` group is similarly fairly balanced between males and females but there is a slightly larger discrepancy. The high school equivalent `education` group is the least balanced, with noticeably more men than females.

### 2.2.2. Distribution of `age` by `sex` & `education`

```{r mims-age-dens}
mims |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = .4, color = "blue") +
  facet_grid(education ~ .) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Age for Men and Females by Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex",
    caption = "Data from NHANES")
```

Based on the **Distribution of Age for Men and Females by Education** density plots, participants with more than high school `education` tend to be younger, and females in this group are especially concentrated in their 30s. Participants with less than high school `education` tend to be older, and the `age` distributions of men and females in this group are similar. In the high school equivalent `education` group, men are spread fairly evenly across ages, while females are concentrated at older ages.

## 2.3. Total Activity

```{r mims-total-scatt}
mims |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(total_mims = sum(mims)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .6) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total activity (sum of MIMS over 24 hours)",
    color = "Sex",
    caption = "Data from nhanes dataset")
```

In all three `education` groups, total activity tends to decline with `age`, especially after about 60 years. This decline is steepest among participants with less than high school `education.` In that group females are slightly more active than males at younger ages, while males are more active between about ages older than 50. In the high school equivalent and more than high school `education` groups, females tend to have higher total activity than males across most of the `age` range, and the difference is largest between about ages 30 and 50 in the high school equivalent group. One man in the more than high school group has a total activity close to zero.

## 2.4. 24-hour Activity Time Courses

```{r mims-time-smooth}
mims |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = sex), se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +                  
  labs(
    title = "24-hr Activity Time Course Plot",
    x = "Time",
    y = "Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex",
    caption = "Data from nhanes dataset") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 240, 480, 720, 960, 1200, 1440), 
    labels = c("12 AM", "4 AM", "8 AM", "12 PM", "4 PM", "8 PM", "12 AM")
  )
```

In every `education` group, activity follows a daily rhythm. It is lowest between about midnight and 5 AM, rises sharply between about 6 AM and 10 AM, stays fairly high through the day, and declines from about 8 PM until midnight. Differences by `sex` are clearest in the high school equivalent and more than high school `education` groups, where females are more active than men during the day (roughly 8 AM to 8 PM). In the less than high school group, males and females have similar daytime activity, but males are somewhat more active late at night and in the early morning. Participants with less than high school `education` also have a slightly higher midday peak than the other two groups.

# Problem 3: Citi Bike

## 3.1. Import, Clean, Tidy, and Merge `citi` Data
```{r citi-wrangle}
citi0120 = 
  read_csv("data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(month = "January", year = "2020")

citi0720 = 
  read_csv("data/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(month = "July", year = "2020")

citi0124 = 
  read_csv("data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(month = "January", year = "2024")

citi0724 = 
  read_csv("data/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(month = "July", year = "2024")

citi = 
  bind_rows(citi0120, citi0720, citi0124, citi0724) |>
  mutate(
    bike_type = case_match(rideable_type,
                           "classic_bike" ~ "classic", 
                           "electric_bike" ~ "electric"),
    bike_type = factor(bike_type),
    weekday = factor(weekdays, levels =c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    ),
    member_status = factor(member_casual),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    year = factor(year)) |>
    select(ride_id, year, month, weekday, duration, member_status, bike_type, start_station_name, end_station_name)
```

## 3.2. `citi` Data Description

`citi` contains data on rides taken on the NYC Citi Bike system in January and July of 2020 and 2024. The dataset includes information on a total of `r nrow(citi)` rides. There are `r ncol(citi)` variables in this dataset, including unique ride ID, duration of ride, names of the start and end station of the ride, type of bike used for the ride, membership status of the associated rider, and each ride's year, month and day of week.

## 3.3. Frequency by `year`, `month`, & `member_status`

### 3.3.1. Tables
```{r rides-freq}
citi |>
  group_by(year, month, member_status) |>
  summarize(rides = n()) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### 3.3.2. Comments
Based on the frequency table, across the years and months observed, Citi Bike members took more rides than casual riders. The `member_status` category that had the combination of years and months recording the greatest frequency were also members and this occurred in `July` of `2024` with 36262 rides. Conversely, the `member_status` category that had the combination of years and months recording the lowest frequency were casual riders and this occurred in `January` of `2020` with 984 rides. 

## 3.4. Frequency among Popular Stations in July 2024
```{r ride_freq_rank}
citi |>
  filter(month == "July" & year == "2024") |>
  group_by(start_station_name) |>
  summarize(rides = n()) |>
  mutate(ride_freq_rank = min_rank(desc(rides))) |>
  filter(ride_freq_rank < 6) |>
  select(-ride_freq_rank) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## 3.5. Effects of `week_day`, `month`, & `year` on `median_duration`
### 3.5.1. Plot
```{r}
citi |>
  group_by(year, month, weekday) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekday, y = median_duration, group = month, color = month)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(year ~ .) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Day of the Week, Month, & Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Duration of Ride",
    caption = "Data from NYC Citi Bike dataset")
```

### 3.5.2. Comments

The plot allows us to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. In `January` of `2024`, `median_duration` was quite relatively consistent throughout the weak, albeit trending upwards from a low of just under `7.5` minutes on `Tuesday` to a high of ~`8` minutes on `Saturday`. On the other hand, in `July` of `2020`, we see a marked difference in `median_duration` across the week, from ~`13` minutes on `Friday` all the way to over `16` minutes over the weekend days of `Saturday` and `Sunday`. That same trend can be appreciated to less exaggerated degree in the other two combinations of `month` and `year`, namely `January` of `2020` and `July` of `2024`, with noticeably higher `median_duration` of rides on `Saturday` and `Sunday`. As alluded to previously, `July` of `2020` saw the highest `median_duration` values across the week, while `January` of `2024` saw the lowest. This leads me to mentioning a clear pattern in `median_duration` of rides in `January` vs `July`. Median duration of rides was higher in `July` than `January`, particularly over the weekends, as mentioned.

## 3.6. Impact of `month`, `member_status`, & `bike_type` on `duration` Distribution
### 3.6.1. Plot

```{r}
citi |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = duration, fill = member_status)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .2, adjust = 1, color = "blue") +
  facet_grid(month ~ bike_type) + 
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Ride Duration",
    x = "Ride Duration (min)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Member Status",
    caption = "Data from the NYC Citi Bike dataset"
  )
```

### 3.6.2. Comments

Based on the density plots, the most stark difference is the distributions of ride `duration` between the two categories of `member_status` among rides taken on `classic` bikes. This difference seems to be that rides taken on `classic` bikes by members are more frequently shorter than rides by casual riders. Otherwise, all 8 of the density plots appear quite right-skewed, with most `duration` values on the short end.
